name: Dietary changes for jaw growth

card.summary: A set of food-texture and eating-habit changes, associated with John Mew's orthotropics, that proponents say load the jaw muscles and guide facial growth toward a more defined jaw and midface.
card.note: Professional orthodontic bodies do not endorse orthotropics; no trial has tested diet alone for jaw shape.

quick.overview:
Dietary changes for jaw growth are the food-related part of orthotropics, the approach developed by British orthodontist John Mew. Its premise is that the texture of what a person eats, and how much chewing it takes, influences how the jaws and face develop. People who follow it hope for a more forward, defined jaw and better-supported midface.
The idea sits alongside tongue posture ('mewing') and palate expansion in Mew's system. Orthodontic organizations describe orthotropics as unsupported by their profession, and no published trial has isolated diet as a way to change adult or child jaw shape.
quick.how: In practice, followers choose firmer, chewier foods over soft or processed ones, so that the jaw muscles work harder at meals, and they often pair this with tongue-posture habits. It is usually discussed as a long-term lifestyle habit, most often for children and teenagers whose faces are still growing, rather than a short course with a fixed endpoint.
quick.risks: Eating firmer foods carries few direct risks beyond jaw or tooth strain in people with existing temporomandibular or dental problems. The main documented concern raised by orthodontists is that relying on orthotropics may delay conventional orthodontic or surgical care in growing children.

lead: Dietary changes for jaw growth refers to eating habits, mainly choosing harder or chewier foods, that followers of orthotropics believe help the jaws and face grow forward and into a more defined shape. The diet component is one of three parts of the approach developed by British orthodontist John Mew, alongside a specific tongue resting position and palatal expansion.[1]

Mew proposed in 1958 'The Tropic Premise', which framed malocclusion as a postural deformity, and built orthotropics after visiting Rolf Fränkel in East Germany in 1968. He argued that environment rather than genetics largely decides whether teeth are crooked, which differs from the mainstream orthodontic view that crowding is mainly genetic.[1] Dietary change is part of how he said the environment could be shaped.

Orthotropics spread widely online from 2019 under the name mewing, and looksmaxxing communities adopted its diet and posture ideas.[2] Professional bodies do not endorse it: Wikipedia reports that the American Association of Orthodontists states there is no evidence mewing improves the jaw, and that a 2019 review in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery found the evidence of efficacy inadequate.[1][2]

chain: Jaw muscles are used more at each meal
Proponents say bone and midface growth follow the load
A more defined jaw and forward-set face
angle.text: Followers swap soft foods for ones that take more chewing, hoping the added muscle use steers jaw and midface growth, especially in childhood. They usually combine it with tongue posture and describe the payoff as a sharper jawline and better facial support.

paras: Orthotropics holds that modern soft diets and mouth-breathing leave the jaws under-used, producing narrow arches and recessed faces. Its dietary advice is to make meals demand more chewing. The wider system also includes a tongue resting position, said to push the upper jaw outward and prevent downward and backward growth, and palate widening with expanders.[1]

Mew summarised the posture side of the approach as 'stand up straight and shut your mouth'.[1] The dietary change is the least formalised element, and it is usually described by followers as a general preference for harder foods rather than a defined protocol.

John Mew (1928 to 2025) qualified in dentistry in 1953, proposed the Tropic Premise in 1958 and developed orthotropics and the Biobloc appliance system after 1968. The International Association of Facial Growth Guidance was founded in 1987.[1]

Interest in 'mewing' rose from January 2019 on social media, and it is closely associated with looksmaxxing subcultures.[2] Diet advice travelled with it as part of the broader jaw-development theory.

Orthodontic organizations and reviewers describe orthotropics as lacking supporting evidence, and most orthodontists do not regard it as an alternative to orthognathic surgery.[1][2] Mew was reprimanded by the General Dental Council in 2010 over advertising claims and had his licence revoked in 2017, per Wikipedia; Wikipedia also reports he was struck from the UK dental register in 2024.[1][2]

Proponents point to the general idea that mechanical loading influences bone, and to anecdotes of changed faces. No controlled study of dietary texture as a stand-alone intervention for jaw shape is known.

timeline.event: John Mew proposes 'The Tropic Premise', framing malocclusion as a postural problem.[1]
Mew visits Rolf Fränkel in East Germany and goes on to develop orthotropics.[1]
International Association of Facial Growth Guidance founded.[1]
Mewing goes viral on social media; a Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery review finds inadequate evidence of efficacy.[1][2]
